title: Requirements distiller and backlog implementor
purpose: Sam and the team need one pipeline that turns loose requirements from any mix of sources into a verified, combined backlog with a decision-led report, and builds that backlog to the same standard on Claude or Codex. It replaces four drivers, three buildability rules and three ruling mechanisms that drifted apart. It is needed now because Codex mode builds worse than Claude mode while Sam's weekly Claude limit keeps running out.

invariants.text: No backlog field says how to build: no files, commands, steps or executor detail. The plan is the only recipe.
invariants.why: R1: an increment is a requirement, never a recipe.

invariants.text: Nothing in the backlog depends on which executor builds it.
invariants.why: R5: the same backlog, unmodified, must build under either executor.

invariants.text: Every increment is a vertical slice of behaviour across every repo it needs; none is one layer of another.
invariants.why: R7: full-stack slices, never one repo at a time.

invariants.text: The four frozen parity corpora and their reports keep working unchanged.
invariants.why: Reshaping the tracked parity backlog breaks tim CI.

invariants.text: Only the writer changes backlog, run-state, run-configuration and phase-ledger files.
invariants.why: Prompt rules do not protect state; a validating writer does.

invariants.text: The review skills' top-level instructions, personas and routing, the rules and the best-practice files are read live by path at run time on either executor, never copied, baked or pinned; a recorded content hash is an audit record and never holds an edit back.
invariants.why: R2 and R3: updates to the skills and rules are picked up automatically.

invariants.text: tim code is tested on its inputs and outputs, uses libraries, and never shells out to gh, jq, curl or the tools scripts.
Every message, report and document is GDS plain British English, with no em dashes and no time estimates.
invariants.why: How Sam wants to be written to.

invariants.text: No design or plan choice rests on build effort, file count, diff size or new surface.
invariants.why: R8: build the right thing; the cost of building it is not a criterion. The plan, the plan audit and the judge each apply it.

direction: Choose the option that is better in use: output quality, requirement and report quality, Codex and Claude parity, full-stack slices, correctness, and operability under the rails. Build effort, diff size and the number of new files carry no weight (R8). Collapsing an overhead that every run pays counts.

questions.headline: What may the judges panel decide without you?
questions.question: When sources disagree and the precedence rules cannot settle it, a panel of three judges and a chair rules. Which rulings may it make on its own?
questions.inPlay: The distiller's panel phase and every conflict it settles. Each panel ruling is listed in the report with how to reverse it.

options.text: The panel rules anything the sources, precedence and your standing rulings can settle. It escalates security, access control, data integrity, legal, policy and scope, anything against one of your rulings, and anything that would change built work.
options.consequence: Fewer questions reach you, and you see every panel call afterwards with how to reverse it.

options.text: The panel only recommends. Every conflict precedence cannot settle comes to you with its recommendation.
options.consequence: More questions reach you; the plants digest needed 8 dockets. Nothing is decided without you.

options.text: No panel. Every conflict precedence cannot settle comes to you as a question.
options.consequence: Saves four agents per docket and a critic, but questions arrive without a recommendation.

questions.headline: What must Codex show before Codex mode is called equal?
questions.question: The parity proof builds three canaries each way and compares them. What result counts as equal?
questions.inPlay: The Codex parity increment, and when Codex mode is offered as equal to Claude.

options.text: The design's bar: identical prompts apart from the profile, nothing unread, the same ladder and acceptance results, the backlog unchanged, and Codex finding at least 90% of Claude's fix-now findings with 80% judge agreement.
options.consequence: A clear pass or fail, but fixed numbers cannot tell "as good" from "worse" without knowing how far two Claude runs already differ.

options.text: The exact checks only; the review and judge numbers are shown but not required.
options.consequence: Codex passes sooner, but a weaker reviewer could pass.

options.text: Codex must match or beat Claude on every measure.
options.consequence: The strictest bar; ordinary variation between runs could fail it.

options.text: A measured bar: the exact checks, plus Codex's fix-now recall and judge agreement falling within the spread between two Claude builds of the same canaries, with 90% and 80% kept as floors.
options.consequence: "As good as Claude" is measured, not guessed, and every failed measure becomes a named fix. It costs one more Claude build of the three canaries.

ifNobodyAnswers.consequence: The proof is judged against option D's measured bar, with the 90% and 80% floors.

blastRadius.why: The comparison can be re-read against another bar without rebuilding.

questions.meanwhile: The parity proof runs; only its verdict depends on the bar.

questions.headline: May other people's words from transcripts, chats and emails be kept in git?
questions.question: Conversational sources carry people's words, names and times. The rule in force keeps your own words in git as a brief, and keeps everyone else's words on this machine, with a paraphrase and a provenance token in git. Should other people's verbatim words ever be kept in the tracked backlog?
questions.inPlay: Every conversational source other than your own brief: meeting transcripts, chat exports, emails and Jira comments by anyone else. Other source kinds are unaffected.

options.text: No. Other people's words stay on this machine; git holds the provenance token and a paraphrase. This is the rule in force.
options.consequence: Nothing personal about anyone else enters git, but other readers cannot check a conversational quote for themselves.

options.text: Yes. Keep other people's words in git like any other source.
options.consequence: Every reader has the full evidence, and other people's words become part of the repository's history, which is hard to undo.

options.text: Do not accept conversational sources at all.
options.consequence: The conversation-sources increment is dropped, and decisions made only in conversation must be written down elsewhere first.

ifNobodyAnswers.consequence: Nothing waits. The rule in force keeps other people's words out of git, and it cannot be relaxed until you rule.

requirements.statement: Every review, verify, judge and fix task MUST read, when it runs and on either executor, the top-level instructions of the review or code-style skill that owns its role, the persona its role follows and the best-practice files the skill's routing names, from the live workspace by path, and a recorded content hash MUST never stop an edit to any of them reaching the next task.
requirements.why: An edit to either skill's method, not only to a persona, must reach every build without a pipeline change.

acceptance.text: Given an edit to the review skill's top-level instructions made after a build run starts, when the next review task runs on either executor, then its reading record shows the edited instructions read in full, and no pipeline file changed.
Given a routed best-practice file edited after a review task was prepared, when that task is accepted, then its receipt names the changed file and the task is accepted, not refused.
Given a skill change that renames a worker or changes a worker's granularity, when the workspace checks run, then one check fails naming the change, and the skill's own change is not blocked.

requirements.falsifiedBy: A review, verify, judge or fix task that ran against a copied, baked or pinned version of either skill's instructions, personas or best-practice files.

requirements.title: Deterministic steps run as tested writer commands, never inside a judgement task
requirements.statement: Every deterministic step of a build or a distillation (branch set-up, merging the base branch, rungs, change lists, scans, stack runs, commits and state writes) MUST run as a tested writer command, and no planning, implementing, reviewing, verifying, judging, fixing or acceptance task MUST run any such step other than accepting its own output.
requirements.why: Deterministic work is scripted and tested once; a judgement task that runs it spends its attention and its tokens on work that has one right answer.

acceptance.text: Given the multi-repo fixture increment built end to end, when every judgement task's commands are read from its transcript or event log, then none ran anything but reading files and accepting its own output.
Given the same run, when the journal is read, then every rung, merge, commit and scan has a fact record the writer wrote, and none rests on an agent's report.

requirements.falsifiedBy: A judgement task whose transcript shows it running a rung, a merge, a commit, a scan or the stack.

requirements.title: One cheap agent runs each gap between judgement stages
requirements.statement: Each run of mechanical steps between two judgement stages MUST be carried out by at most one agent that runs only the commands the decision command gives it, and the number of such agents MUST NOT grow with the number of repos, rungs, shards or files.
requirements.why: Every agent has a fixed start-up cost in tokens and wall-clock that every increment pays, so the agents, not the stages, are the cost of a run.

acceptance.text: Given fixture increments touching one repo and three repos, with one rung and six rungs and three shards, when both are built, then both spend the same number of such agents, one per gap between judgement stages.
Given an increment whose reviews find nothing, when it is built, then no verify, judge, fix or fix-verify task runs and no agent is spent for them.
Given an increment with every model role bound to Codex, when the journal is read, then at most two agents were spent on it.
Given a run launched on a fixture, when the journal is read, then exactly one agent ran before the first judgement task, and it ran only the decision command.

requirements.falsifiedBy: A build whose agent count per increment rises with its repos, rungs, shards or files, or a gap between judgement stages that spent more than one agent without a handback.

requirements.title: Every outward action is its own call, and its result is read back
requirements.statement: Every push, pull request creation, merge and ticket write MUST be its own shell call that names what it does, and the build MUST establish its result by reading the remote state, never from a relayed exit code.
requirements.why: These actions are hard to reverse and seen by other people, so each must stay visible to the per-call hooks, and a relayed exit code can be wrong.

acceptance.text: Given the land step on the fixture, when it finishes, then no remote branch has moved until the separate push calls run.
Given a push reported as failed that in fact reached the remote, when the next step is asked for, then it is recorded as pushed and not pushed again.
Given a checkout on main, or a push that is not a fast-forward of the remote branch, when push commands are generated, then none is generated and the increment is held.

requirements.falsifiedBy: A push, pull request, merge or ticket write made inside another command, or recorded from an agent's report without reading the remote state.
